newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Bank reform delay may hamper Tanzania loans.
newsitem.headline: Bank reform delay may hamper Tanzania loans.

text.p: Delays in reforming Tanzania's state-owned National Bank of Commerce (NBC) may hamper loans under the Structural Adjustment Credit, Western diplomats and Tanzanian financial officials said on Monday.
Presidential spokesman Patrick Chokola told Reuters reforms in the bank would be delayed until September to allow the government to study other available options for privatisation.
The World Bank credit is worth $125 million.
"The main issue is (that) it will allow more time for the government to look at other strategies. Up to now there's only been one -- to split the bank into three," he said.
"Other strategies should be considered to allow more analysis. This is a sensitive issue," Chokola said.

The timetable for the NBC break-up had orgininally been set for July 1. Following the end of the budget review in August, it was expected that parliament would approve changes to the 1972 Public Corporations Act which would formally enable Mkapa to implement the restructuring proposals.

Diplomats said World Bank Director James Adams told Tanzanian President Benjamin Mkapa at a weekend meeting in Tanzania that lack of details on a timetable for NBC reforms threatened 125 million in Structural Adjustment Credit (SAC).

"Next week the World Bank has to go to its executive board to get it (SAC) approved. They (World Bank) won't until they get details. Adams said: we're not going to move forward until we get details on their (government) timing (for restructuring)," one senior diplomat added.

An emotive issue surrounding the bank's privatisation is the fate of an estimated 2,000 employees among the NBC's total workforce of 4,000. Other questions being asked by those opposed to the bank's break-up is the cost of the restructuring and details about the proposed new banking operations.
Diplomats said the two-month breathing space would allow Mkapa and his reformist Finance Minister, Daniel Yona, to "convert the doubting Thomases" about the government plans.

Restructuring the NBC, Tanzania's largest commercial bank, is a thorny issue for Mkapa, amid strong opposition from supporters of the bank established in 1967 under the socialist blueprint policies of founding president Julius Nyerere.
"The process of internal political consensus building has not been attended to. There is a need for legal action," said one senior diplomat familiar with the NBC wrangles.
The senior representative of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in Tanzania, Festus Osunsade, said that the IMF had no reason to doubt the government's promises to break up the NBC.
"The government has assured us about their commitment to restructure and privatise the NBC and we're waiting for the necessary government action to this effect," he said.
Several local newspapers last week claimed that Nyerere, strongly opposed the restructuring of the NBC into three subsidiary banks comprising trade, regional and micro-finance.
